meta.title: Who really said "What Is the Difference Between a Misfortune and a Calamity?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The Gladstone-in-the-Thames joke is a French template documented from 1861. Disraeli’s name was attached only in 1887, after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What Is the Difference Between a Misfortune and a Calamity?'?
meta.ogDescription: Probably not Disraeli. The joke is documented in 1861 about Napoleon III’s cousin and the Seine; the Thames version arrives in 1887.

answer.label: Probably not Disraeli — a French joke he would have been borrowing
answer.authorDates: Documented from 28 May 1861 · first told of Disraeli in 1887
answer.sourceLine: The riddle and its punchline were circulating in France and Britain for a quarter of a century before anyone put them in Disraeli’s mouth. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest instance to The Leeds Mercury of 28 May 1861, where the Emperor tells his son that it would be an accident if Prince Napoleon fell into the Seine, “but it would be a misfortune if any one were to help him out again.” The version with Gladstone and the Thames first appears in 1887; the exact misfortune/calamity wording quoted here first appears in Meynell’s 1903 biography ↗.

source.heading: Where the joke actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Travelling joke template, French in origin
Wilfrid Meynell, Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography, 1903, p. 146

source.excerpt: “What is the difference between a misfortune and a calamity?”—somebody asked a new definition from Disraeli. The questioner, being no literalist, but a man of liberal understanding, got the reply: “Well, if Gladstone fell into the Thames, that would be a misfortune; and if anybody pulled him out, that, I suppose, would be a calamity.”
trail: The earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ locates ran in The Leeds Mercury on 28 May 1861 and presents the joke as French: the Emperor explains to his son that it would be an accident if his cousin Prince Napoleon tumbled into the Seine, “but it would be a misfortune if any one were to help him out again.”

The template kept moving. Punch ran it in January 1867 as dinner-party banter, first naming the politician John Bright and then swapping in the host of the party; in November 1880 the London paper Truth aimed it at Gladstone, but the teller was an unnamed Conservative lecturer, not Disraeli, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Disraeli died in 1881. The first version attached to him appeared in January 1887 in The Dial of Chicago, and used the words “mischance” and “misfortune” rather than the pairing quoted here, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The wording on this page — misfortune against calamity — first appears in Wilfrid Meynell’s biography of 1903, page 146, which we read in the scanned edition ↗. Meynell offers no source; H. L. Mencken later dated the remark to about 1867, also without a citation.
source.excerptNote: As printed in Wilfrid Meynell, Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography (New York: D. Appleton, 1903), page 146 — the earliest appearance of this exact wording. We read the passage in the scanned edition ↗. Meynell gives no source for the anecdote.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: About the author — and why there isn’t one
author.metaLine: Unidentified · earliest documented instance in The Leeds Mercury, 28 May 1861
author.bio: The joke has no known author. It appears first as a French story about Napoleon III and his cousin, reaches British print in 1861, and is retold for the next fifty years with whichever public figure the teller wished to see drowned. Disraeli is one of at least six victims, and the only reason his version survived is that his biographer printed it in 1903.

misattribution.heading: Did Disraeli really say it?
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication in the usual sense — it is a joke that existed before Disraeli was credited with it, and that was told about at least six different victims. He may well have used it. What cannot be shown is that he invented it, or that he said these words.

items.why: Every telling that names Disraeli is posthumous. The earliest, in The Dial of January 1887, comes six years after his death in 1881 and carries no source; Meynell’s 1903 book, the origin of this exact wording, gives none either, per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Wikiquote lists it as a sourced Disraeli quotation
items.why: We disagree with a specialist here, so it should be said plainly: Wikiquote’s Disraeli page ↗ carries this line under “Sourced but undated”, citing Wilfrid Meynell’s 1903 biography, page 146. That citation is real, but it is not independent corroboration — Meynell’s book is itself the earliest known appearance of this wording, published 22 years after Disraeli died, and it names no source. The joke is documented from 1861, per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: An anonymous French joke, documented 28 May 1861
items.why: The Leeds Mercury printed it in 1861 as a story told in France about Napoleon III and his cousin, with the Seine standing in for the Thames. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the template originated in France and that The Leeds Mercury and Punch popularised it in Britain.

items.who: Prince Napoleon, John Bright, Mr Snippson, a mother-in-law, Lloyd George
items.why: The victim changes with the audience: Prince Napoleon (1861), the politician John Bright (1867), a pressing tailor (1880), Max O’Rell’s mother-in-law (1883) and David Lloyd George (1913). Quote Investigator ↗ reads the variability as deliberate retuning to whoever the teller disliked.

misattribution.truthLine: It is conceivable Disraeli told this joke about Gladstone, but the evidence is weak and he would have been using a template that was already twenty years old, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Disraeli and Gladstone loathed each other with a thoroughness that made them the best-documented political rivalry in Victorian Britain, and the joke stuck to them because it fits — it is exactly the kind of thing readers wanted Disraeli to have said. That is the mechanism by which a stock gag becomes a historical quotation.

The riddle form is what makes it portable. Because the setup is a question about two words, only the name in the punchline has to change, and the joke survives translation from the Seine to the Thames without losing anything.
detailsBody: The pairing of words drifted along with the victim. Quote Investigator ↗ records accident against malheur, accident against misfortune, mischance against misfortune, mishap against misfortune, and finally misfortune against calamity — the version Meynell printed in 1903 and the one that survives today.

H. L. Mencken included the anecdote in A New Dictionary of Quotations on Historical Principles, ascribing it to Disraeli about 1867 and adding that similar sayings had been aimed at many statesmen since. He supplied no citation for the date, and no earlier Disraeli instance has since been found.
context.pull: Only the name in the punchline has to change.
